title: Switzerland confirms first cyberattacks using AI agents, including on infrastructure
excerpt: Switzerland's cyber security office says AI agents were used in five confirmed attacks, three on critical infrastructure operators. No major outages were reported. Italy issued a similar alert.

sources.title: SRF: Fünf bestätigte Fälle - Erstmals Cyberangriffe mit KI-Agenten in der Schweiz
SWI swissinfo.ch (Keystone-SDA): Erste Cyberangriffe auf kritische Infrastruktur mit KI-Agenten

eSecurity Planet: Switzerland Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattacks, Urges 24-Hour Patching

body_html:
Switzerland's Federal Office for Cyber Security (BACS, also known by its former name, the National Cyber Security Centre) has confirmed the country's first known cyberattacks carried out with the help of AI agents. AI agents are programs that can plan and carry out a series of steps on their own, such as searching for weak spots and trying passwords.

What happened

BACS published a warning on Tuesday 24 November 2026, as reported by swissinfo.ch and eSecurity Planet. It said organisations had been attacked, including operators of critical infrastructure in at least two sectors. Critical infrastructure means services society depends on, such as electricity, water and telecommunications.

On 26 November, BACS director Florian Schütz told Swiss public broadcaster SRF: "We currently have five confirmed cases of attacks using AI agents" (our translation). All were reported in recent days. Three of the five involved critical infrastructure operators. Smaller businesses that reported attacks voluntarily were also affected. According to SRF, no major outages have been reported.

BACS says the attackers used AI programs to look for weaknesses, such as easily guessed passwords and known software flaws, and to carry out attacks with little human input. The programs can do this far faster than a person and switch methods when defences react, which leaves organisations much less time to notice and respond.

Italy's national cyber security team, CSIRT Italia, issued a separate bulletin dated 23 November describing campaigns in which several AI agents working in parallel broke into many systems within a few hours, according to The Hacker News and eSecurity Planet. In October, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security had already warned that agentic AI was speeding up attacks, while noting that humans still choose the targets.

What is still unknown

  • Who was attacked: BACS has not named the organisations or the exact sectors. It says those affected have the right to speak for themselves.
  • Who is behind it: the attackers have not been identified.
  • How many attacks succeeded: reports differ. SRF reports that systems were breached in four of the five cases; swissinfo.ch and watson report two successful attacks. The BACS warning itself could not be opened for this story.
  • What happened after the break-ins: whether data was taken or systems were changed has not been reported.
  • Which tools were used: BACS has not said which AI tools were involved in the Swiss cases.

What BACS recommends

As reported by SRF, swissinfo.ch and watson, BACS advises organisations to:

  • keep as few systems as possible reachable from the internet;
  • install critical security updates as fast as possible, and on internet-facing systems within 24 hours of release;
  • use multi-factor authentication everywhere, and strictly limit who can access what;
  • check their own systems for weaknesses regularly, themselves or with outside specialists.

Which Directives cover this risk

Attacks like these succeed through familiar gaps: weak passwords, missing updates and systems left open to the internet. That is the territory of Directive 6: Secure and supported, which asks that products get timely security updates for as long as they are in use. The same agent technology that attackers misuse is also being built into products people buy, so Directive 2: Bounded autonomy and Directive 1: Always stoppable matter on the defending side too: an agent should only reach what it needs, and people must be able to stop it. As we say on our security page, a hacked robot is one nobody is in charge of.

Questions you can ask any maker

  • How quickly do you ship security fixes, and for how many years?
  • Does the product or its control account support multi-factor authentication or passkeys?
  • Which parts of the product are reachable from the internet, and can I turn them off?
  • If your product includes an AI agent, what can it access, and how do I stop it?

More questions are on our questions to ask page. Incidents like these are a reason for clear, independent security standards, not a reason to fear the technology itself.
